prompt: I run a small ceramics studio called Kiln & Fern in Asheville. Can you build me a one-page homepage hero (name, one line about what we do, a button to book a studio visit, and three small cards for Classes, Shop, Visit)? It has to be a single HTML file with inline CSS, no external fonts or images, since I'll just email it to my web guy. I want it to feel warmer and more modern than the usual pottery site.
rubric: The page loads no external fonts, stylesheets, scripts or images and uses only fonts a visitor's device already has, listed as a stack with sensible fallbacks.
The studio name and headline carry a recognizable personality in the type (a deliberate choice of face, weight or style) rather than looking like the browser default.
No more than two type families are in play, and each has a clear job (for example display versus reading), with the card labels and button text matching one of them.
The headline, one-liner, button and card titles are clearly different in presence from each other, and body-sized text stays comfortably readable in the screenshot.
The warm, modern feel comes from the type and layout working together, not from decorative script or novelty faces.

prompt: We're building Ledgerline, billing software for small law firms. The product UI is currently all in one default sans and the marketing site feels bland. I'd like a heading and body font pairing but we can't load web fonts yet because legal needs to review licenses, so it has to be fonts people already have on Mac, Windows and phones. What would you go with?
rubric: Gives a concrete pick for headings and for body (named families or stacks), not a list of general qualities.
Every recommended family is one that ships with common operating systems, and the answer gives fallbacks for the platforms that lack it.
Explains why the pair suits a trustworthy professional audience in terms a founder could repeat, without leaning on vague words like clean or modern alone.
Is honest about the limits of system fonts (they differ between platforms, so the page will not look identical everywhere) and says what to check or what could be upgraded once licensing is cleared.
Does not recommend a face that exists only on one platform as the sole choice, and does not pad the answer with a long catalog of alternatives.
Identifies that too many families with overlapping roles are competing, and ties that to the messy feeling patients report.
Gives a concrete, shortened replacement set (a specific number of families with named jobs) rather than only saying use fewer fonts.
Addresses the audience: older patients reading appointment details, including what that means for body face legibility or phone-number presentation.
Points out something specific in the supplied CSS, such as the monospace phone number or the repeated serif/sans swaps between heading levels, instead of generic font advice.
Offers a practical fallback or loading consideration (web fonts missing, system alternative) in a sentence or two without turning into a tutorial.
Recognizes the setup is already sound and says so plainly rather than inventing problems.
Does not recommend replacing the families or rebuilding the system; any suggestion is small, optional and clearly marked as minor.
Notes at least one thing that is working for a concrete reason (for example the serif for long reading, or tabular figures for the tide table).
Any change suggested is accurate and low-risk, and the answer is short enough to read as a quick check, not a redesign.
Does not pad with a list of trendier alternative fonts the user did not ask about.

prompt: Build me a simple internal page for our warehouse team at Brightwater Freight: a table of 8 or so inbound shipments with columns for shipment ID (like BW-20418), carrier, dock door, ETA and status. Single HTML file, inline CSS, no external anything. People will have it open on a shared monitor all day and need to scan IDs quickly. Please pick good fonts for it.
rubric: The page is one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS that loads nothing external.
The type choice fits a utility screen: a plain, legible system sans (or a single sans) for most text, without forcing a decorative display face or a heading and body pairing for its own sake.
Shipment IDs and times are easy to scan and compare, for example by using a monospaced face or aligned figures, so that characters like 0 and O or 1 and l cannot be confused.
Numeric columns line up cleanly in the screenshot, and status text is distinguishable without needing a different font for each column.
Uses at most two families and does not add a branded or editorial typeface to a tool meant for reading from across a room.

prompt: My designer sent me a font file called Marlowe-Variable.ttf for the new site I'm building for my bakery. I've heard 'variable font' a lot but don't really get it. What is it, is it better than the normal kind, and am I actually allowed to put it on my website? I'm not very technical.
rubric: Explains in plain language that a variable font holds a range of weights or widths in one file, with at least one concrete benefit or tradeoff (fewer files, smooth weights, or file size).
Does not oversell variable fonts as always better; it names when a single static file or system font is just as good.

Is honest that it cannot tell from the file name whether the licence allows website use, and says the desktop licence often differs from web use and that the user should check the licence or ask the designer or foundry.
Gives a short practical next step the user can take (what to ask the designer, where to look in the licence, what format to use for the web).
Stays at a level a non-technical bakery owner can follow, without code or jargon left undefined.

prompt: We run an app for Cobalt Straits Ferries. Timetables and alerts need to show in English, Arabic and Japanese, and also include stop names in Latin script inside the Arabic and Japanese text. I'm laying out the alert card and the departures list this week and I don't want any of the three scripts to look like an afterthought. How should I handle the fonts?
rubric: Treats each script as needing its own font (or system face) selection with fallbacks, rather than picking one Latin font and hoping the others fall back.
Gives a concrete font-stack approach for mixed text, including how Latin stop names embedded in Arabic or Japanese should be handled so they match the surrounding text's visual weight and size.

Mentions at least two script-specific practical concerns, such as Arabic needing different size or line spacing than Latin, Japanese needing a font that actually contains its characters, or right-to-left direction for the Arabic card.
Is honest about what cannot be guaranteed on system fonts across devices, and says what to test or which platform gaps to expect.
Stays focused on the typeface decisions for the cards and list, without turning into a general localization or layout engineering guide.

prompt: Wedding site for Inés and Tomás, mostly photos, a schedule, and an RSVP form. They want it romantic but not cheesy and not a script font. What font should I use for the names at the top? Please answer in two sentences max, I just need to tell my cousin who's building it.
rubric: Answer is no longer than two sentences.
Names one specific recommendation for the headline names, not a menu of several options.
The recommendation respects the brief: romantic in feel and clearly not a script or novelty face.
Includes a fallback or note that works if the cousin cannot load the font, or says it is available without installing anything.
Does not add a preamble, a bulleted list or an unrequested explanation of type theory.
Diagnoses that the figures have different widths in this font (proportional figures) and that this causes the misaligned digits, rather than blaming the alignment or layout.
Gives a specific fix the user can paste, such as tabular figures via font-variant-numeric or the equivalent, applied to the price and seat columns.
Keeps the existing humanist sans, as the user asked, and does not suggest switching families as the main fix.
Is honest that tabular figures depend on the font supporting them, and says what to do or expect if the fallback font does not.

Mentions that right alignment with consistent decimals or digit counts is also needed for the digits to line up, or otherwise shows an accurate understanding that figure width is the cause but alignment still matters.

prompt: Make me a single HTML page (inline CSS, no web fonts, no images, nothing external) for a late-night radio show called Low Tide Radio: show title, tagline, tonight's 4-item playlist with artist and track, and a 'Listen live' button. The vibe is after-midnight, a little literary, a little analog. Don't make it look like every other dark-mode music page.
rubric: The page is a single self-contained HTML file that loads nothing external and relies on fonts a device already has, with fallbacks.
The type gives the title a distinctive, literary or analog character using available system faces (for example a serif with presence), instead of defaulting to a standard UI sans for everything.
The playlist separates artist from track title through typographic means such as weight, style or case, so each line parses at a glance.
Type choices rather than gradients or effects deliver the after-midnight mood, and the page does not look like a generic dark-mode music template.
No more than two families are used, text on the dark or tinted ground stays readable in the screenshot, and the button label matches the page's type system.
